name: Propanediol

lead: Propanediol is a small two-hydroxyl molecule used in serums, moisturizers and makeup to hydrate skin, improve texture and help other ingredients dissolve and spread. Two forms are used: 1,2-propanediol (propylene glycol) and 1,3-propanediol, often made by fermentation and sold as a plant-derived alternative.

As a humectant it binds water, and as a solvent and penetration enhancer it helps other ingredients dissolve and move into the upper skin layers, according to encyclopedic descriptions. It is a supporting ingredient in the base of products rather than a treatment, and no human trial has tested it as a standalone appearance treatment.

paras: People get it as part of the base of serums, moisturizers and makeup rather than on its own. It often lets actives feel lighter and spread more evenly.

Toxicity is described as low, but contact allergy is reported in an estimated 0.8 to 3.5 percent of people depending on concentration. Propylene glycol was the American Contact Dermatitis Society's 2018 Allergen of the Year.

angle.text: Propanediol hydrates skin and helps other actives dissolve, absorb and spread, giving a smoother-feeling, better-delivered skincare routine. It is chosen as a plant-derived alternative to propylene glycol.

lead: Propanediol is the name for a small group of organic compounds with the formula C3H8O2 in which two hydroxyl groups sit on a three-carbon chain. Two isomers matter commercially: 1,2-propanediol, better known as propylene glycol, and 1,3-propanediol, which is often made by fermentation and sold in cosmetics as a plant-derived alternative.[1][2]

In skin care both isomers appear as solvents, carriers and humectants, meaning ingredients that attract and hold water and help dissolve other actives. They are rarely the focus of a product; they are listed on labels as part of the base of serums, moisturisers and makeup.[1][2]

No published human trial has tested propanediol as a standalone appearance treatment. Its safety profile is described by encyclopedic sources as low in toxicity, with allergic contact dermatitis reported in a small share of people; the American Contact Dermatitis Society named propylene glycol its 2018 Allergen of the Year.[2]
infobox: Cosmetic ingredient; propylene glycol is FDA GRAS as a food additive[2]

paras: Propanediol has four constitutional isomers, but only the 1,2- and 1,3- forms are industrially significant; the geminal forms (both hydroxyls on one carbon) are unstable.[1] 1,2-Propanediol is a viscous, nearly odourless liquid miscible with water and many solvents, and its molecule is chiral, although commercial material is typically a racemic mixture.[2] 1,3-Propanediol is a straight-chain diol with a boiling point of about 214 C.[1]

Propylene glycol is made mainly from propylene oxide, with annual output reported at around 2 million tonnes. 1,3-Propanediol can be made chemically or by microbial fermentation of glycerol or glucose, a route that has been the subject of metabolic-engineering research.[1][2][3]

Encyclopedic sources describe propylene glycol as a common carrier and base in makeup and as a humectant in products such as alcohol-based hand sanitisers, where it helps limit drying of the skin.[2] 1,3-Propanediol is described as a humectant, solvent and penetration enhancer in cosmetic and personal care formulations, marketed as a more renewable option.[1]

A US drug label on DailyMed lists a topical product from the brand Anubis Barcelona combining propanediol, glycerin and magnesium ascorbyl phosphate, marketed with a 'Botox-like' description. The label gives no efficacy data.[4]

Propylene glycol is also a food additive, a solvent in oral, injectable and topical medicines, an ingredient in e-cigarette liquids and theatrical fog, and a lower-toxicity substitute for ethylene glycol in some antifreezes. 1,3-Propanediol is chiefly a monomer for the polyester polytrimethylene terephthalate.[1][2]

Reported acute oral toxicity of propylene glycol is low; toxicity has mainly been described after very high blood levels, often following large intravenous doses. Undiluted contact has been described as causing minimal, transient eye irritation.[2]

Estimated prevalence of allergic reactions ranges from roughly 0.8 percent to 3.5 percent depending on concentration, and propylene glycol was named Allergen of the Year by the American Contact Dermatitis Society in 2018.[2] The US FDA lists it as generally recognised as safe for food use, and the European Food Safety Authority has set an acceptable daily intake of 25 mg per kg of body weight.[2]

No studies found on propanediol as a cosmetic anti-ageing or appearance treatment. Registered trials in which propylene glycol appears are about other things: a pharmacokinetic study in healthy adults,[5] and studies of ocular emulsions or lubricating eye products in which it is a component or comparator vehicle.[6] Those do not test skin appearance outcomes.
